what_it_does: Multiplying two sparse matrices (matrices where most entries are zero — common in graph analytics and some AI workloads) is much harder to parallelize than multiplying dense matrices, because the locations of non-zero values are irregular. One popular approach on GPUs uses hash tables stored in the GPU's small but very fast on-chip shared memory (a scratchpad visible to a group of threads) to accumulate partial products, but hash collisions slow things down and the memory often sits underused. HSMU-SpGEMM redesigns the hash-based accumulator so it keeps the fast shared memory as full as possible while reducing collisions, and also improves the two preparatory counting steps (estimating how many non-zeros will appear in the result) that precede the actual multiply. The approach is evaluated across three GPU generations.
